newsitem.title: USA: US Tax negotiators see progress, Clinton letter.
newsitem.headline: US Tax negotiators see progress, Clinton letter.

text.p: Congressional tax negotiators said some progress was made in a Saturday meeting on tax cut legislation with White House emissaries who brought a letter of guidance from President Clinton.

"I think we had a very good meeting with the administration and I think we're making some progress, it's slow, nothing's been agreed upon, nothing's final, but we're making a little progress," Assistant Senate Majority Leader Don Nickles, an Oklahoma Republican, said.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin led the administration team in the tax negotiations, and at one point the meeting room was cleared of all staff-level aides while the main negotiators spoke in private.

Clinton's letter spelled out his requirements for the tax bill and was addressed to Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican. "I want to highlight the fundamental principles that must be met in any tax cut package that I sign into law," Clinton wrote.

House and Senate tax negotiators are trying to work out differences in their respective bills and craft a compromise that the president will sign into law. The legislation would enact the part of the May budget agreement between congressional leaders and the White House calling for $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years.

Neither the House nor Senate bill provided an adequate share of tax relief to middle-income families, Clinton wrote. The fairness issue has dominated the tax debate, with Democrats saying Republican plans give too much tax relief to the wealthy, and Republicans saying their bills largely benefit the middle class.

Clinton said the congressional bills also failed the fairness test by denying a full $500 per-child tax credit to low-income working families who receive the earned income tax credit. Republicans say the child credit should not go to people who do not pay taxes otherwise it would be welfare.
Clinton also said the House and Senate tax bills "fall substantially short" of the roughly $35 billion in tax breaks for college education agreed to in the budget pact.

The president criticised provisions in both bills that he said would "explode in cost" in later years. He cited capital gains "indexing" which would take into account effects of inflation and so would lower the taxable amount of profits on investments. Clinton also referred to "substantial estate tax changes" and "unconstrained" Individual Retirement Accounts.
"While we strongly favour reasonable expansion of IRAs for retirement and education savings, the IRAs in the House and Senate bills are simply too expensive in the decades to come," Clinton wrote.

Tax negotiators characterised Saturday's meeting as an exchange of views, but no resolutions yet. "We're not at the stage of resolving, we're at the stage of discussing," John Hilley, White House legislative director said.
"I thought the meeting tonight was very productive and constructive, we're going to continue them tomorrow," Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said.
"They feel like they broke through an impasse at this meeting," Ginny Flynn, a spokeswoman for Roth, said later.
Negotiators were discussing the six biggest items that amounted to $120 billion to $130 billion over five years, House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, said.

On Friday, Roth put a discussion proposal on the table that dealt with the six -- the $500 per-child tax credit, education tax incentives, expanded Individual Retirement Accounts, a capital gains tax cut, estate tax relief, and alternative minimum tax relief. It was unclear what the status of his proposal was after Saturday's meeting.
